canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Evaluating a Bilinear Form
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the the bilinear form $B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}),$ given by 

$$
B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})= 2 x_1y_2 - x_2y_2 +3 x_2y_3-x_3y_1
$$

 

Evaluate $B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})$ when ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124253/assets/e355ba8664f980f8e06bcbda40adf063d376478e745b9b6b036331a895192c54.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124253/assets/7fe125bd6366adb85e10ab5719049e1e0db7c719b4a714f9155efee77a8f604b.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We are given that 

$\qquad$ ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124253/assets/14418dfa570c1be7015799f009ad93388a6dd6d04bed48972bc8163351bbeb87.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124253/assets/8bc4748c7c554dc1edfbdce567f9e6d994ebe0955346bfa34712e20286aaa3b3.svg) 

Substituting these into the bilinear expression, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}B(x,y) & =2{x}_{1}{y}_{2}-{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+3{x}_{2}{y}_{3}-{x}_{3}{y}_{1} \\  & =2\cdot 1\cdot 2-1\cdot 2+3\cdot 1\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot (-2) \\  & =4-2+3-2 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
The matrix of the bilinear form $B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) = 2x_1y_1 + 2x_2y_1 - x_3 y_2+2x_3y_3$ is given below. What is the value of $a+b+c?$

$$
[\begin{aligned}a & 0 & 0 \\ b & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & c & 2\end{aligned}]
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Each term $a_{ij}x_i y_j$ in the expression of the bilinear form corresponds to the entry $a_{ij}$ of the matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(x,y) & =2{x}_{1}{y}_{1}+2{x}_{2}{y}_{1}-{x}_{3}{y}_{2}+2{x}_{3}{y}_{3} \\  & =2{x}_{1}{y}_{1}+0{x}_{1}{y}_{2}+0{x}_{1}{y}_{3} \\  & +\,2{x}_{2}{y}_{1}+0{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+0{x}_{2}{y}_{3} \\  & +\,0{x}_{3}{y}_{1}+(-1){x}_{3}{y}_{2}+2{x}_{3}{y}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, the corresponding matrix of the bilinear form is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124253/assets/443b1cf1d4425f83b834101627dd202732cf2c905848c8ddbb93dd518f3b35db.svg)

Therefore, $a=2,$ $b=2,$ and $c=-1.$ Finally, 

$$
a+b+c=2+2+(-1) = 3.
$$

tutorials.problem:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. A  function 

$$
f: \Bbb R^n \to \Bbb R
$$

is a **linear form**  (or  *linear functional*) if there is a row-vector 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124253/assets/952d8832a903cf184286698e449da84d94d61cb46d984a48f33f406a42a8007a.svg)

such that for any ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124253/assets/6b756f37311a5e7f4e6cfb160a37b31d54b2ce1e29849044101dc82d49e44d21.svg) we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =ax \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & ⋯ & {a}_{n}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={a}_{1}{x}_{1}+{a}_{2}{x}_{2}+…+{a}_{n}{x}_{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

For example, let $f(\mathbf{x})$ be the linear form   defined on $\Bbb R^2$ by $f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{a} \mathbf{x},$ where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124253/assets/26cf6eb0836041b648c29908c8d13ae132e644ea68c772e81e011470283c3427.svg)

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =ax \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\,1 \\ \,\,-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =3\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot (-1) \\  & =3+2 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. A  function 

$$
f: \Bbb R^n \to \Bbb R
$$

is a **linear form**  (or  *linear functional*) if there is a row-vector 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124253/assets/952d8832a903cf184286698e449da84d94d61cb46d984a48f33f406a42a8007a.svg)

such that for any ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124253/assets/6b756f37311a5e7f4e6cfb160a37b31d54b2ce1e29849044101dc82d49e44d21.svg) we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =ax \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & ⋯ & {a}_{n}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={a}_{1}{x}_{1}+{a}_{2}{x}_{2}+…+{a}_{n}{x}_{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

For example, let $f(\mathbf{x})$ be the linear form   defined on $\Bbb R^2$ by $f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{a} \mathbf{x},$ where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124253/assets/26cf6eb0836041b648c29908c8d13ae132e644ea68c772e81e011470283c3427.svg) 

Suppose we want to evaluate $f(\mathbf{x})$ at ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124253/assets/5d6ebda5e8563d23b66cdf15f4a47a1ae712510eeacbe6bcebd031534bcc841a.svg) Then, we simply substitute ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124253/assets/6c79170289a47e3ebb2a7226432938640c63ccea0d032e674d4f03967c12c8ea.svg) and obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =ax \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\,1 \\ \,\,-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =3\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot (-1) \\  & =3+2 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Bilinear Forms
tutorials.problem:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. A  function $B: \Bbb R^n\times \Bbb R^n \to \Bbb R$ is said to be a **bilinear form** if there is an $n\times n$   matrix $A$ such that 

$$
B(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) =  \mathbf{x}^T \! A\mathbf{y}, \qquad  \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \Bbb R^n.
$$

Suppose, for example, that ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124253/assets/e3ef7815e373c266abf34e4bbba1dd9b29adf2865721afeb8bf4e3eb44b105dc.svg) To  evaluate the bilinear form $B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{y}$ when ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124253/assets/ac7f10624ad2b9d0807018976526311423dc4110a98ba24f4ff7eac6760af616.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124253/assets/5a074c9193bbe395506549cb69b1b2e84d1208211efb1008a5192989850606ce.svg) we substitute  these vectors in the above expression as follows 

$$
\begin{aligned}B(x,y) & ={x}^{T}\,Ay \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

 

To write down our bilinear form $B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})$ above in terms of vector components 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124253/assets/c47fc6c2d7df7ced599a643531bc19656c7c62915930583089df641e493680e5.svg)

we proceed as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}B(x,y) & ={x}^{T}\,Ay \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}+2{y}_{2} \\ 3{y}_{1}+4{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}({y}_{1}+2{y}_{2})+{x}_{2}(3{y}_{1}+4{y}_{2}) \\  & ={x}_{1}{y}_{1}+2{x}_{1}{y}_{2}+3{x}_{2}{y}_{1}+4{x}_{2}{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.title: Bilinear Forms
tutorials.content:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. A  function $B: \Bbb R^n\times \Bbb R^n \to \Bbb R$ is said to be a **bilinear form** if there is an $n\times n$   matrix $A$ such that 

$$
B(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) =  \mathbf{x}^T \! A\mathbf{y}, \qquad  \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \Bbb R^n.
$$

Suppose, for example, that ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14124253/assets/e3ef7815e373c266abf34e4bbba1dd9b29adf2865721afeb8bf4e3eb44b105dc.svg) To  evaluate the bilinear form $B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! tutorials.name: Properties of Bilinear Forms
tutorials.problem:
Suppose $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix. Then, it readily follows that the function $B: \Bbb R^n\times \Bbb R^n \to \Bbb R$ defined as 

$$
B(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) =  \mathbf{x}^T \! A \, \mathbf{y}, \qquad \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \Bbb R^n,
$$

is **linear in each argument** separately. That's the reason why we call them *bilinear*.

- For $\mathbf{y}$ fixed, all $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \Bbb R^n,$  and any real constant $c$, linearity in the first argument means the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(u+v,y) & =B(u,y)+B(v,y) \\ B(cu,y) & =c\,B(u,y)\end{aligned}
$$

- For $\mathbf{x}$ fixed, all $\mathbf{w}, \mathbf{z} \in \Bbb R^n,$ and any real constant $c$, linearity in the second argument means the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(x,w+z) & =B(x,w)+B(x,z) \\ B(x,cw) & =c\,B(x,w)\end{aligned}
$$
